kh:body.core:para: This Overview is a guide to the Lexis+® UK Financial Services subtopic Sanctions compliance and includes links to appropriate materials. UK sanctions obligations apply to all businesses and persons in the UK; this sub-topic focuses on the implications for firms regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA 2000), cryptoasset firms registered with the FCA under the Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017, SI 2017/692 (MLRs), and payments and e-money firms supervised by the FCA (herein referred to as firms), in their compliance with sanctions.

tr:secmain.core:title: What are international sanctions?
tr:secmain.core:para: Sanctions regimes are a tool of foreign policy affecting businesses or persons and are typically used where international peace and security is threatened. They can:

core:listitem.core:para: encourage a change in the behaviour, policy or activity of the target person, entity, government or country
apply pressure on a target to comply with certain objectives, and
enforce measures where diplomatic efforts have failed

tr:secmain.core:para: Sanctions regimes are reviewed, lifted, revoked or adapted in the light of changes in the behaviour of the target. They will typically have been created by one of the following: the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), the Council of the EU under its Council Common Foreign and Security Policy, the US Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), or by the UK government.

Sanctions measures include financial sanctions (such as asset freezes), trade sanctions (such as arms embargoes), transport sanctions and immigration sanctions (such as travel bans), in addition to export controls.

tr:secmain.core:title: Sanctions and the FCA
tr:secmain.core:para: FCA Webpage: Financial sanctionsThe Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) is not responsible for enforcing sanctions, but it does expect regulated firms’ systems and controls to mitigate the risk of financial crime and meet their obligations under sanctions. It expects the same of firms not regulated under FSMA 2000, but supervised by the FCA such as e-money and payment firms and cryptoasset businesses.

The Practice Note: Introduction to UK sanctions compliance for financial services firms introduces the UK financial sanctions framework as it applies to financial services firms. It provides an overview of:

core:listitem.core:para: FCA and PRA regulatory requirements of firms and senior management in relation to sanctions including the FCA’s Principles for Business, Senior Management Arrangements, Systems and Controls sourcebook and the Conduct Rules
relevant guidance (and its scope and status):

core:sub1listitem.core:para: the FCA’s Financial Crime Guide (FCG)—FCG 2 and FCG 7
the FCA’s Financial Crime Thematic Reviews (FCTR)—FCTR 8, FCTR 12, FCTR 15 and FCTR 16
the Joint Money Laundering Steering Group Guidance—Part III, Chapter 4 on compliance with the UK financial sanctions regime
the Wolfsberg Group’s Guidance on Sanctions Screening

core:listitem.core:para: systems and controls expected of the FCA
the relationship between the MLRs, the AML/CTF framework and sanctions

tr:secmain.core:para: For information on trade sanctions and weapons proliferation, see below.

tr:secmain.core:title: Systems and controls to prevent financial sanctions evasion
tr:secmain.core:para: Detailed consideration of the regulatory requirements and guidance for financial services firms expected of the FCA is set out in the following Practice Notes:

lnci:cite.lnci:content: Financial sanctions systems and controls —financial services
Sanctions screening for financial services firms
Sanctions reporting obligations for financial services firms

tr:secmain.core:para: The Practice Note: Financial sanctions systems and controls—financial services addresses the FCA's requirements and expectations for a firm's financial sanctions systems and controls in relation to:

core:listitem.core:para: risk assessments
policies and procedures
governance and senior management responsibility
management information
resource provision
communication, training and staff awareness
international sanctions compliance

tr:secmain.core:para: This Practice Note: Sanctions screening for financial services firms sets out the FCA’s expectations of firms’ sanctions systems and controls in relation to:

core:listitem.core:para: sanctions screening policies and procedures
automated sanctions screening tools
sanctions screening of customers, counterparties and payments
customer due diligence checks relevant to sanctions
timing of sanctions screening
escalation of target matches and ‘false positives’
managing the customer relationship following a true match
outsourcing sanctions screening
evasion detection and investigation
asset freezing and licences
audit trail and record-keeping
historical reviews (lookbacks)
common misconceptions around sanctions screening identified by the FCA

tr:secmain.core:para: The Practice Note: Sanctions reporting obligations for financial services firms sets out:

core:listitem.core:para: legal and regulatory reporting obligations
reporting process
the FCA’s expectations of formal reporting to OFSI and filing suspicious activity reports when necessary
reporting to the FCA when the firm/connected person is a sanctions target
reporting to the FCA when there is an actual or suspected sanctions breach
reporting to the FCA of weaknesses in a firm’s sanctions systems and controls
relationship between reporting to OFSI, the FCA and submitting a SAR
the FCA’s Annual Financial Crime Report (REP-CRIM) as it relates to sanctions

tr:secmain.core:title: FCA supervision and enforcement action for financial sanctions breaches
tr:secmain.core:para: The Practice Note: FCA supervisory and enforcement focus on sanctions compliance considers: priority areas and sectors for FCA supervision, including the regulators’ statements and feedback in light of geopolitical developments, the FCA’s sanctions screening tool and FCA enforcement action for breaches or weaknesses in sanctions compliance. Traditionally the UK regulators are more powerful enforcers than OFSI. A breach of sanctions requirements is also likely to result in a regulatory breach. The Practice Note considers:

core:listitem.core:para: FCA supervision of firms’ sanctions systems and controls, including the FCA’s sanctions screening tool
priority areas and sectors for FCA supervision, including the regulators’ statements and feedback in light of geopolitical developments and sectoral portfolio letters
the relevance of sanctions compliance to the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA)
FCA (and PRA) enforcement action for failures around sanctions compliance, and
the 2025 Financial Services Threat Assessment Report published by the Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI) which may indicate potential areas of FCA focus

tr:secmain.core:para: Information on previous FCA enforcement relating to sanctions and to AML/CTF breaches can be found in the Lexis+® UK Financial Services Enforcement Database using Keywords including: ‘Sanctions compliance’ and ‘Financial crime compliance'. The database incorporates detailed information on all substantive FCA and PRA Final Notices and, where available, Decision Notices from 2014 onwards. It may be searched and filtered by fields including rule breach, sector, date, seriousness, aggravating and mitigating factors, financial penalty, and other actions such as referrals to the Upper Tribunal.

tr:secmain.core:title: Systems and controls to prevent trade sanctions evasion and weapons proliferation
tr:secmain.core:para: The Practice Note: Trade sanctions and proliferation financing systems and controls for financial services firms focuses on the implications of trade sanctions and weapons proliferation for financial services firms. It is particularly relevant to those firms which conduct trade finance, project finance and insurers. This Practice Note addresses the FCA's requirements for a firm's trade sanctions and counter proliferation financing (CPF) systems and controls and guidance set out in the FCA’s Financial Crime Guide (FCG) 7 and the FCA’s Financial Crime Thematic Review (FCTR) 15.
The Practice Note considers:

core:listitem.core:para: FCA regulatory requirements and guidance
overview of UK trade sanctions and PF framework as it applies to financial services firms
systems and controls—weapons proliferation
regulatory considerations for firms conducting trade finance, and
overlap between trade sanctions and AML/CTF measures

tr:secmain.core:title: UK sanctions framework
tr:secmain.core:para: The Sanctions and Anti-money Laundering Act 2018 (SAMLA 2018) enables the UK to implement sanctions post-Brexit and to update existing provisions on anti-money laundering (AML) and counter terrorist financing (CTF), giving the government powers to make regulations:

core:listitem.core:para: to impose sanctions to comply with UN and other international obligations
to create exceptions and licences to allow activities to take place that would otherwise be prohibited or restricted by sanctions
to update existing provisions on anti-money laundering and terrorist financing—particularly the MLRs
to prevent terrorism
for national security or international peace and security

tr:secmain.core:para: With the UK effectively replacing the EU legislation with SAMLA 2018–based statutory instruments, a significant body of legislation has been laid. Further information can be found in Practice Note: The UK sanctions framework under SAMLA 2018.

tr:secmain.core:title: UK financial sanctions
tr:secmain.core:para: Financial sanctions can range from the comprehensive prohibition of the transfer of funds to a target country and freezing of government assets to particular sanctions targeting specific individuals or entities. The sanctions apply to all financial transactions. There is no minimum financial threshold and the sanctions may also apply to financial advice. For further information, see .

The Office of Financial Sanctions (OFSI) within HM Treasury maintains a Consolidated List of financial sanctions targets designated by the United Nations, the EU and the UK; this list is updated regularly.

It is a criminal offence not to comply with a financial sanction unless you have an appropriate licence or authorisation from the OFSI. For relevant General Licences issued by the Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI) under the UK financial sanctions regime, see Practice Note: OFSI General Licence tracker.

If firms become aware of a breach, they must notify OFSI in accordance with the relevant provisions. OFSI have published guidance on complying with UK obligations and this is available here. At the earliest opportunity, in circumstances including where: it knows or suspects that a breach of financial sanctions has occurred; a regulated firm is also expected to notify the FCA (see Practice Note: Sanctions reporting obligations for financial services firms).

tr:secmain.core:title: UK trade sanctions
tr:secmain.core:para: Trade sanctions prohibit the trade of certain goods from affected countries. Trade sanctions are relevant for financial services firms as they generally prohibit the provision of financial services in connection with the restricted trade. Commonly trade sanctions prohibit the direct or indirect provision of financial services, and the direct or indirect making available of funds, to persons connected with arrangements captured by the trade sanction.
For further information on trade sanctions, see Practice Note: Understanding the UK trade sanctions regime.

tr:secmain.core:title: Counter-proliferation
tr:secmain.core:para: From 1 September 2022, firms in the scope of the Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017, SI 2017/692, (MLR 2017) must assess proliferation financing risks and put in place policies, controls and procedures to mitigate and manage those risks. The regulatory framework around counter-proliferation is based upon sanctions, export controls and AML/CTF regimes. For further information on counter-proliferation, see Practice Notes: Introduction to the UK AML/CTF/CPF legal and regulatory framework for financial services—What is money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing? and The Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing (Amendment) (No.2) Regulations 2022—one minute guide for financial services [Archived].

tr:secmain.core:title: Offences relating to financial sanctions
tr:secmain.core:para: In the UK, the offences relating to financial sanctions include offences relating to dealing with the funds or economic resources of a designated person or entity, or transacting with such a person or entity. The substantive prohibitions/offences are essentially the same in each sanctions regime (although there are occasional exceptions, such as the asset freeze imposed on the funds of the Libyan Investment Authority and Libyan Investment Africa Portfolio, which is narrower in scope). The offences are set out under the Terrorist Asset-Freezing etc Act 2010 (TAFA 2010). For more information, see Practice Note: Financial sanctions—offences.

tr:secmain.core:title: Financial sanctions toolkit
tr:secmain.core:para: The Financial sanctions toolkit brings together resources from across Lexis+® UK to provide insight and practical guidance on UK and international regimes for financial sanctions. In includes introductory content explaining the different sources of sanctions, the different types of sanctions which may be imposed, the specific sanctions regimes operating under SAMLA 2018, explains which government departments are responsible for the implementation and enforcement of sanctions, the offences that can be committed and the other enforcement options available following breach including monetary penalties. It also brings together key materials on financial sanctions compliance as well as sector specific guidance for financial services firms, law firms, banking and finance lawyers and insurance lawyers.

The toolkit includes practical guidance on specific sanctions regime such as Practice Notes: Sanctions regime—Russia, Sanctions regime—Belarus, Sanctions regime—cyber, Sanctions regime—global anti-corruption, and Sanctions regime—global human rights.

tr:secmain.core:title: International sanctions
tr:secmain.core:para: Other countries impose their own sanctions regimes of which UK businesses need to be aware if they are trading in these jurisdictions. Information on international sanctions regimes can be found in Practice Notes:

lnci:cite.lnci:content: Designation of sanctions targets under the UN sanctions, UK sanctions and EU sanctions regimes

tr:secmain.core:para: The Economic Crime (Transparency and Enforcement) Act 2022 allows sanctions to be rapidly imposed against persons already designated by allies, as well as intensifying sanction enforcement. Details of the Act can be found in Practice Note: Economic Crime (Transparency and Enforcement) Act 2022—an introduction.

tr:secsub1.core:title: EU sanctions
tr:secsub1.core:para: The EU imposes sanctions and embargoes to further its Common Foreign and Security Policy objectives. They are implemented through the European Council or the European Commission regulations which are directly applicable in all Member States.

EU sanctions generally relate to designated individuals or entities (Designated Persons) and other specific controls directed at specific industries or sectors. They prohibit EU Persons from making funds or economic resources available, directly or indirectly, to or for the benefit of a Designated Person. There is a further requirement on EU Persons to freeze funds owned, held or controlled by a Designated Person. The Practice Note EU sanctions compliance for financial services firms, provides a detailed and practical overview of the EU sanctions framework as it applies to financial services firms. It explains how EU financial sanctions, particularly asset freeze measures, affect the activities and compliance obligations of banks, payment service providers and other financial institutions, including sanctions screening and transaction controls. It also outlines the role of licences and exemptions and the enforcement of EU sanctions. It further examines how sanctions compliance is expected to be integrated into firms’ wider AML/CTF governance and risk frameworks, and considers the role of national competent authorities, the EBA’s sanctions guidelines and the role of the EU’s Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA).
For more information, see Practice Notes: Designation of sanctions targets under the UN sanctions, UK sanctions and EU sanctions regimes and International sanctions—an introduction.

tr:secsub1.core:title: US sanctions
tr:secsub1.core:para: The Office of Foreign Assets Control of the United States Department of the Treasury (OFAC) administers US economic and trade sanctions. OFAC publishes a list of individuals and companies owned or controlled by, or acting for or on behalf of, targeted countries. It also lists individuals and entities that are not related to a particular country. Collectively these are listed on the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons list (SDN List).

US sanctions have a broad reach and apply globally to 'US Persons'. The OFAC also enforces sanctions requirements against non-US persons in relation to transactions involving US Persons or the US financial system. It also prohibits US Persons from facilitating transactions by non-US persons if it would be illegal for a US Person to directly undertake such transaction.
Undertaking any type of business or financial transaction with a sanctions target is illegal under US federal law and may result in civil or criminal liability and substantial fines and imprisonment.

tr:secsub1.core:title: Country guides and comparator tool
tr:secsub1.core:para: The Lexology Panoramic guides in relation to international sanctions provide an overview of individual jurisdictions’ approach to sanctions. The International comparator tool is designed to allow lawyers to compare legal differences across two or more jurisdictions in any given practice area. Using information from the Lexology Panoramic Guides, it can generate answers to your comparison requests. This is a valuable aid to uncover issues in cross-border matters and multi-jurisdictional issues. The International comparator tool can be accessed in Practice Note: Lexology Panoramic: Sanctions.

tr:secmain.core:title: Precedents
tr:secmain.core:para: Links to sector neutral precedents relating to policies and also to specific procedures, including screening and alerts, reporting breaches, staff awareness and training and monitoring and review may be found in: Sanctions compliance—overview.
